period: Christian kingdoms from the 6th century; Islamic Nubia from about the 14th century
summary: Christian Nubian kingdoms that beat back the Arab armies, signed a treaty that lasted 600 years, and wrote their own language in Greek letters.
look: This section shows medieval Nubia: church objects and crosses, boldly painted pottery, inscriptions in Greek, Coptic and Old Nubian, and Islamic tombstones. The great wall paintings of the cathedral of Faras are mostly in Warsaw and Khartoum; if a painting fragment is on show here, its label will say where it came from.
story:
When Kush collapsed in the 4th century, three kingdoms took its place: Nobatia in the north, Makuria around Dongola, and Alodia in the south. In the 6th century rival missions from Constantinople, one backed by Justinian and one by his wife Theodora, raced to convert them. Probably in the 7th century Makuria absorbed Nobatia and reached as far north as Philae.

In 651-652 an Arab army under Abdallah ibn Saad besieged Dongola and bombarded it with catapults but could not take the citadel; Muslim sources praise the skill of the Nubian archers. The two sides agreed the Baqt: an annual exchange of Nubian slaves for Egyptian wheat and textiles, later expanded to protect travellers on both sides. Makuria was recognised as independent, and the Baqt lasted, with interruptions, for more than six centuries.

From the 9th to the 11th century Makuria flourished: churches covered in murals, fine painted pottery, and documents in Old Nubian, written in a Greek-based alphabet with extra signs, and readable today. The Polish team that excavated the cathedral of Faras in the 1960s rescued its paintings. Pressure from Mamluk Egypt, internal conflict and changing trade brought decline; Muslim kings ruled Dongola briefly in the 1310s and 1320s, and over the following centuries most Nubians became Muslim.
details: Old Nubian writing: letters that look almost Greek, with a few extra signs.
Christian-period pottery painted with bold birds, fish and geometric bands.
Crosses on stone, bronze or pottery from Nubian churches now under the lake.
Islamic tombstones in angular Kufic Arabic script, like those of Aswan's Fatimid cemetery.
fun_fact: Arab writers nicknamed the Nubians 'the pupil smiters', because their archers could hit an enemy in the eye.
narration:
For a thousand years after the pyramids of Meroe, Nubia was Christian. In the 6th century missionaries from Constantinople converted its kingdoms, and the strongest, Makuria, came to rule from Dongola as far north as Philae.

Then came a famous standoff. In 652 an Arab army marched south from newly conquered Egypt and besieged Dongola with catapults. It could not take the citadel. Arab writers nicknamed the Nubian archers the pupil smiters, because they aimed for the eyes. So both sides made a deal called the Baqt: every year Nubian slaves went north and Egyptian wheat and cloth went south. With interruptions, it lasted for more than 600 years.

Makuria flourished. Its cathedral at Faras was covered in paintings, rescued in the 1960s by Polish archaeologists. Nubians wrote their own language, Old Nubian, in a Greek-based alphabet that scholars can still read. From the 14th century the kingdom weakened and Nubia slowly became Muslim. Look for writing that looks almost Greek but not quite: that is likely Old Nubian.

period: Traditional Nubian life; resettlement after the dams, 1902-1964
summary: Painted vaulted houses, waterwheels and wedding songs, and the photographs of the 1960s, when a whole people left their valley to a lake.
look: The last galleries show traditional Nubian life in life-size scenes: a mud-brick house with a decorated facade, a waterwheel, a wedding, crafts and jewellery. Photographs show the old villages before Lake Nasser.
story:
Nubians are not a vanished people: they are Aswan's neighbours. In Egypt the main groups are the Kenzi, who speak Kenzi, and the Fadija, who speak Nobiin, a descendant of the medieval Old Nubian language. Further south in Sudan live the Halfawi, Sukkot, Mahas and Danagla.

Their villages once lined the river between Aswan and the Second Cataract, on a narrow strip of farmland watered by the saqiya, an ox-driven waterwheel lifting pots of water to the fields. Houses were built of mud brick with vaulted or domed roofs and big courtyards, their facades whitewashed and painted with patterns, birds or boats, some with china plates set into the walls. This architecture fascinated the Egyptian architect Hassan Fathy, who later designed the Aga Khan's villa here.

Each raising of the old dam drowned villages, and families rebuilt higher up. The High Dam ended that: about 100,000 Nubians in Egypt and Sudan were displaced, and in Egypt the Kenzi and Fadija were resettled in 'New Nubia' villages near Kom Ombo, away from the river. For many families the move is still living memory, and today many Nubians live in Aswan, Kom Ombo and Cairo.
details: The house reconstruction: look for the vaulted roof and the painted decoration around the door.
The saqiya: an ox turns a wheel that raises a chain of pots from the river.
Photographs of villages before the lake: compare them with Gharb Soheil today.
Silver and gold jewellery: a bride's wealth worn on her body.
fun_fact: Nubian builders roofed rooms with mud-brick vaults raised without wooden scaffolding, leaning each course against the last, a trick Egyptians already used in the Ramesseum's granaries 3,000 years ago.
narration:
These last rooms bring Nubia up to living memory. The Nubians are not a lost people: they are Aswan's neighbours, and many still speak their own languages, Kenzi and Nobiin, at home.

Look at the house. Nubian homes were built of mud brick, with vaulted or domed roofs raised without wooden scaffolding, a big courtyard, and a facade whitewashed and painted with patterns, birds or boats. Some had china plates set into the walls.

The waterwheel, the saqiya, was turned by oxen, lifting pots of water to the fields along the narrow strip of the valley. Weddings went on for days, with drums, clapping and songs.

Then look at the photographs. Each raising of the old dam drowned villages, and families rebuilt higher up. The High Dam finished the job. About 100,000 Nubians in Egypt and Sudan had to leave, and in Egypt many were resettled in new villages near Kom Ombo, away from the river. Find a photograph of a village before the lake, and picture it now under water.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, possibly Hatshepsut's reign, about 1479-1458 BC
summary: The biggest obelisk ever attempted, still lying in its quarry: about 42 metres and some 1,090 tonnes, abandoned when the granite cracked.
look: From walkways you look down into an open granite quarry. The obelisk lies on its back, its upper faces and sides cut free, its underside still part of the bedrock. A crack runs across it. Around it are the workers' trenches, their walls scooped into rounded hollows by pounding, and here and there faint ochre lines. There is no shade: come early.
story:
Finished, it would have stood about 41.75 metres tall and weighed nearly 1,090 tonnes, nearly a third larger than any obelisk Egypt ever raised. The largest standing today, the Lateran Obelisk in Rome, originally from Karnak, is 32.2 metres and 455 tonnes. Nobody signed this one, but it is often attributed to Hatshepsut, possibly as a partner to the Lateran obelisk; you will see her surviving obelisk at Karnak on the 22nd.

It shows the whole method. Quarrymen outlined the shape, then pounded the granite away with balls of dolerite, a stone harder than granite, working shoulder to shoulder in trenches around the block. Their marks, and the ochre lines marking the work, are still visible. Reginald Engelbach studied the site in detail in 1922. The next stage would have been to undercut the obelisk, free it from the bedrock, drag it to the river and float it north on the flood.

Then cracks appeared in the granite and the project was abandoned. It is a rare snapshot of a monument caught halfway. In 2005 an unfinished obelisk base and rock carvings were found elsewhere in the Aswan quarries, which are protected as an open-air museum.
details: The crack running across the body of the obelisk: the reason it was abandoned.
The trench walls: rows of rounded scoops left by dolerite pounders.
Faint ochre lines on the stone, where overseers marked the work.
The underside, still part of the bedrock: the cut that was never made.
Look at the pointed end: you can judge the full length from tip to base.
fun_fact: The word obelisk is Greek: obeliskos means 'little spit', a skewer for roasting meat. A cheeky name for a thousand tonnes of granite.
narration:
Below you lies the largest obelisk anyone ever tried to make, and it never left the ground. If it had been finished, it would have stood about 42 metres tall and weighed around 1,090 tonnes, nearly a third bigger than any obelisk the Egyptians ever raised. The largest one still standing today, in Rome, is about 32 metres.

Nobody signed it, but it is often thought to have been ordered by Hatshepsut, the woman who ruled as king, perhaps to pair with a giant obelisk at Karnak.

What makes it precious is that it shows the method. The workers did not cut this with iron tools. They pounded the granite with balls of dolerite, a stone even harder than granite, crouching shoulder to shoulder in trenches around the shape. Look at the trench walls: the rounded scoops are their pounding marks. You can still find faint ochre lines where the work was marked out.

Then cracks appeared in the granite, and the whole project was abandoned, with the underside still attached to the bedrock. Had it worked, they would have cut it free underneath, dragged it to the river, and floated it north on the flood.

Walk round until you can see the crack across the body of the obelisk. Then look again at the scalloped trench walls: every hollow is the work of human arms.

period: Worked from the Early Dynastic period to Roman times, and still today
summary: The hard red and black stone of Egypt's grandest monuments, from Khufu's burial chamber to the obelisks of Rome, came out of these hills.
look: Around the Unfinished Obelisk and along the east-bank hills, look for worked granite: flat cut faces, trenches, and rows of rectangular slots where blocks were split with wedges. The stone is a coarse pink-red granite speckled with black, with grey and darker varieties too.
story:
Aswan granite was Egypt's luxury stone: hard, colourful, able to take a mirror polish and almost indestructible. The quarries on both banks supplied colossal statues, obelisks, sarcophagi and monolithic shrines across Egypt, and the pyramid builders used it for their most important rooms: the burial chamber of Khufu's Great Pyramid is built of it, and so are the great blocks of Khafre's Valley Temple. A road was cut beside the quarries from Syene to Philae.

Moving it was the hard part. Blocks were dragged on sledges to the river and loaded onto barges, ideally when the flood was high, then floated north.

Cutting it took patience. In earlier times quarrymen pounded trenches around a block with balls of dolerite, which is harder than granite; in later periods, especially Roman times, they cut a row of slots, drove in wedges and split the stone. How the Egyptians raised obelisks is still debated; one theory has the obelisk hauled up an earth ramp and lowered, base first, into a sand-filled pit as the sand was let out.

The Greek name syenite comes from Syene, and some quarries are still worked today.
details: Rows of rectangular slots along a rock edge: wedge holes for splitting granite.
Rounded scoops in trench walls: the marks of dolerite pounders.
Look closely at the stone: pink feldspar crystals, grey quartz and black flecks.
From the quarry, look at the surrounding hills: the whole ridge is the same granite.
fun_fact: If you went inside the Great Pyramid on the 12th, the King's Chamber you stood in was made of granite from these hills, carried the length of Egypt by river.
narration:
The rock around you is Aswan granite, Egypt's luxury stone. It is hard, it takes a mirror polish, and it almost never wears away. That is why pharaohs wanted it for their most important work: obelisks, colossal statues, sarcophagi, and the burial chamber deep inside Khufu's Great Pyramid at Giza, which is built of blocks from these hills.

Getting it there was the hard part. Blocks were dragged on sledges to the river and loaded onto barges, ideally when the flood was high, then floated north the whole length of Egypt.

Look at how it was cut. In early times, quarrymen pounded it with balls of dolerite, an even harder stone, wearing trenches around the block. Later, they cut a row of slots along a line, hammered in wedges and split the rock. Both kinds of marks survive here.

The Greeks named the stone after the town: syenite, from Syene, the Greek name for Aswan. Find a row of neat rectangular slots on a rock edge nearby: that is where someone set out to split a block, perhaps 2,000 years ago.

period: Old and Middle Kingdom, about 2300-1800 BC; used from Dynasty 4 to the Roman period
summary: The governors of Egypt's frontier, buried in the cliff above the river: explorers, a son who rescued his father's body, and statues in the rock.
look: On the west bank opposite Aswan, rows of rock-cut tomb doorways line terraces below the summit, where a small domed sheikh's tomb gives the site its name, the Dome of the Wind. Steep stairs climb from the landing. Which tombs are open varies, but they usually include Sarenput II and the double tomb of Mekhu and Sabni; Harkhuf's inscribed facade is nearby. Bring water and a torch.
story:
About 100 tombs have been found here, used from the Fourth Dynasty to the Roman period. Most belong to the governors of Elephantine and the expedition leaders they sent south. Their tomb inscriptions record trading voyages and military campaigns, and are some of the earliest travel writing in the world.

The most dramatic is the double tomb of Mekhu and his son Sabni, of the Sixth Dynasty. Mekhu led a royal expedition south and was killed in Nubia. Sabni raised a force, went south, punished those responsible and brought his father's body home for burial.

The best preserved is the tomb of Sarenput II, governor under Amenemhat II and Senusret II in the 12th Dynasty: a pillared hall, then a corridor with niches holding statues of Sarenput in the form of Osiris, and at the end a painted niche with figures of the governor, its colours still fresh.

Digging goes on. The University of Jaen in Spain has worked here since 2008, ten mummified crocodiles were found in 2019, and three new Old Kingdom tombs were announced in 2025.
details: Sarenput II: the corridor niches with statues of Sarenput as Osiris, wrapped like a mummy.
At the back of Sarenput II's tomb: the painted niche, its colours still bright.
Mekhu and Sabni: a double tomb with rough pillars cut from the living rock.
At the top, the sheikh's dome; the view back over Elephantine is one of Aswan's best.
fun_fact: In 2019 archaeologists here found ten mummified crocodiles, up to 3.5 metres long, more than 2,500 years old and preserved without resin.
narration:
You are climbing to the tombs of the men who ran Egypt's southern frontier. About 100 tombs are cut into this cliff, and the little dome on the summit, the tomb of a Muslim holy man, gives the hill its name, Qubbet el Hawa, the Dome of the Wind.

Most belong to governors of Elephantine in the Old and Middle Kingdoms, between about 2300 and 1800 BC. These men led caravans and soldiers into Nubia, and their walls tell of it.

The most moving story belongs to Mekhu and his son Sabni. Mekhu died on an expedition in Nubia. Sabni gathered troops and donkeys, went south, punished those responsible and carried his father's body home to be buried here, beside his own tomb.

The best preserved is the tomb of Sarenput the Second, a governor around 1900 BC. After the pillared hall, a corridor runs into the rock, lined with statues of Sarenput as Osiris, and at the end is a niche painted in colours that still look fresh.

Before you go inside, turn around. Elephantine, the town these men governed, lies right below you.

summary: An explorer who brought back a dancing pygmy, and a boy-king's excited letter telling him to check on him ten times a night.
look: Harkhuf's tomb is in the Qubbet el-Hawa cliff. Its fame is carved on the outside: 58 lines of text in soft, flaking stone around the entrance, with prayers above the door, his journeys on either side, and the king's letter in a long block on the far right.
story:
A native of Elephantine, he served kings Merenre and Pepi II as governor and overseer of caravans. He led four expeditions to Yam, a land probably south of modern Khartoum, though some place it in the Libyan desert. The first was with his father. He boasts of routes no one had used before, of winning over the ruler of Yam, and of returning with 300 donkeys loaded with incense, ebony, oil, panther skins, ivory and other fine goods.

On the fourth journey he brought back a dancing pygmy and sent word ahead. The reply came from Pepi II, still a child: come north at once; bring the pygmy alive and well; put good men around him on deck so he does not fall in the water; have them sleep around him in his tent; inspect ten times a night. His majesty wanted to see this pygmy more than the gifts of the mines of Sinai and of Punt. Harkhuf was so proud that he had the letter carved on his tomb.

His inscription also lists his virtues: he gave bread to the hungry, clothing to the naked, and ferried those who had no boat.
details: The long inscription framing the doorway: 58 lines telling Harkhuf's life.
On the far right of the facade: the king's letter, 26 lines of royal excitement.
Above the entrance: prayers for offerings and Harkhuf's titles.
Look south from the terrace: the direction all four of his caravans set off.
fun_fact: Harkhuf's moral code, 'I gave bread to the hungry, clothing to the naked', was carved more than 4,000 years ago and still sounds like a modern charity appeal.
narration:
This tomb belongs to Harkhuf, one of the first explorers in history. He was from Elephantine, and more than 4,200 years ago he led four caravans deep into Africa, to a land called Yam, probably beyond Khartoum. On one trip he came home with 300 donkeys loaded with incense, ebony, ivory and panther skins.

But the best part is a letter. On his fourth journey Harkhuf brought back a dancing pygmy, and sent word to the palace. The reply came from King Pepi the Second, still a child, and it is wonderfully childlike. Come north at once! Bring the pygmy alive and well! When he goes on board, put good men around him so he does not fall in the water. When he sleeps, have men lie around his tent. Check on him ten times a night! My Majesty wants to see this pygmy more than all the treasures of Sinai and Punt.

Harkhuf was so proud of that letter that he had it carved for eternity. Look at the far right of the doorway and find the long block of text: that is the king's letter.

summary: A Fatimid-style tomb on the desert hill for the leader of the Ismaili Muslims, where a red rose was laid every day.
look: On the west-bank hilltop stands a pink limestone building with a large central dome on an octagonal drum, four small corner domes, crenellated walls and a single arched door on the west side. Below it near the water is the villa where the Aga Khan wintered. The interior has been closed to visitors since 1997; you see it from the river.
story:
Sir Sultan Muhammed Shah, Aga Khan III, was hereditary imam of the Ismaili Shia Muslims and a well-known figure of the 20th century. He wintered in Aswan in a villa designed by Hassan Fathy and asked in his will to be buried near it. He died in 1957, was first buried in Switzerland, and was reburied here on 20 February 1959 before more than 2,000 guests.

His widow, Begum Om Habibeh, commissioned the mausoleum. The Egyptian architect Farid Shafi'e modelled it on Fatimid buildings, above all the 11th-century Juyushi mosque in Cairo. The choice was deliberate: the Fatimid caliphs who founded Cairo were Ismailis. The tomb inside is of Carrara marble.

The Begum began the custom of laying a red rose on the tomb every day. She died in 2000 and is buried beside her husband, and in February 2025 his grandson and successor, Aga Khan IV, was buried here too.
details: From the river: the central dome and the four small corner domes.
The crenellated parapet along the walls, a Fatimid touch.
Below the hill near the water: the villa, designed by Hassan Fathy.
Compare the dome with the Fatimid buildings you saw in Cairo on the 16th.
fun_fact: The design copies the Juyushi mosque on the Muqattam hills in Cairo, built in 1085, so a medieval Cairo silhouette now overlooks the Nubian Nile.
narration:
On the hilltop across the river is the mausoleum of the Aga Khan, the pink building with one large dome and four small ones at the corners.

Aga Khan is the title of the hereditary imam of the Ismaili Muslims, a branch of Shia Islam. The third Aga Khan, Sultan Muhammed Shah, was a famous figure of the 20th century, a statesman and a racehorse owner, and he spent his winters here in Aswan. He died in 1957 and asked to be buried near his villa, the house you can see near the water below.

The tomb was designed to look like a building from Fatimid Cairo. That was no accident. The Fatimid caliphs who founded Cairo more than a thousand years ago were Ismailis, the Aga Khan's spiritual ancestors.

His widow, the Begum, started a custom: every day a red rose was laid on his tomb. She is buried here too, and in 2025 so was his grandson, the fourth Aga Khan. The inside is closed to visitors. Look for the small corner domes, and the crenellated wall along the top.

period: Coptic, founded about AD 571; abandoned after 1321
summary: A fortified desert monastery for some 300 monks, with a painted Christ in its apse, abandoned for 700 years behind the Aga Khan's hill.
look: From the boat landing below the Aga Khan's mausoleum, a sandy path climbs a dry valley to the monastery, about 650 metres from the river; camels are usually on offer. Inside walls over 6 metres high, the site steps up two rock terraces: the church on the lower one, and on the upper the three-storey keep with the monks' cells, the refectory, kitchen and workshops. Visitors enter by the east gate.
story:
Older Coptic and Arabic sources call it Deir Anba Hadra, after a 4th-century hermit who became bishop of Syene; the name of St Simeon came later and was adopted by travellers and archaeologists. Building began around 571. In the 10th century it was renewed and enlarged to house about 300 largely self-sufficient monks, with a mill, oil and wine presses, a bakery, stables and kilns.

The church was a three-aisled basilica; in its apse are the remains of Christ enthroned between two angels. In the refectory, seven rings of mud brick on the floor served as seats.

Saladin attacked in 1173 and badly damaged it. Bedouin raids and water shortages followed, and in 1321 attackers destroyed it, killed many monks and drove out the rest. It was never rebuilt.
details: The church apse: faded remains of Christ enthroned between two angels.
The keep: three storeys, with the monks' cells opening off the dormitory.
The refectory: seven rings of mud brick on the floor that served as seats.
Near the oil press: a granite millstone carved with three crosses.
From the upper terrace: open desert in every direction, the reason for the high walls.
fun_fact: The monastery's cemetery holds nearly 200 gravestones, most from the 6th to 9th centuries.
narration:
You are inside the walls of a desert monastery that has stood empty for 700 years. Later travellers named it after Saint Simeon, but older sources call it after Anba Hadra, a hermit who became bishop of Aswan in the 4th century. Building began around AD 571, and at its height, in the 10th century, about 300 monks lived here behind walls over 6 metres high, with their own mill, oil press, wine press and bakery.

In 1173 Saladin attacked. Bedouin raids and water shortages followed, and in 1321 it was destroyed and abandoned. Find the church apse: the faded figure of Christ enthroned between two angels is still there.

summary: Two dams that ended the Nile flood: harvests and electricity for Egypt, a lake that drowned Nubia, and silt trapped where the fields can't reach it.
look: From the top of the High Dam you see Lake Nasser to the south and the river running towards Aswan to the north. The dam is 3.8 km long, 111 m high, 980 m wide at the base and 40 m at the crest: a mountain of rock and clay, not a concrete wall. At the western end stands the tall lotus-shaped monument to Soviet-Egyptian friendship. The old dam lies 7 km downstream.
story:
The British built the first dam across the Nile at Aswan in 1898-1902, designed by Sir William Willcocks and opened on 10 December 1902. It was raised twice but held too little water to stop the cycle of floods and droughts.

In 1952 the Greek-Egyptian engineer Adrian Daninos proposed a giant dam, and the new government adopted it. The US and Britain offered loans, then withdrew in July 1956; a week later Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal, partly to pay for the dam, and the Soviet Union provided credit, engineers and machinery. Construction began on 9 January 1960 and was completed on 21 July 1970; the lake was full by 1976. The Soviet engineer Nikolai Malyshev designed it, and Egyptian contractors, led by Osman Ahmed Osman's Arab Contractors, built it with some 25,000 Egyptian engineers and workers.

The gains are real: floods and droughts no longer decide the harvest, water is stored over several years, fields can carry two crops a year, and the turbines generate electricity. So are the costs: the silt that once fertilised the valley now settles in the lake, farmers depend on fertiliser and the Delta coast is retreating, and about 100,000 Nubians lost their homeland. The reservoir, Lake Nasser, is about 500 km long.
details: Look south: Lake Nasser, about 500 km long, reaching into Sudan.
Look north: the narrower river and, 7 km away, the old British dam.
The lotus tower at the west end: five petals, a monument to Soviet-Egyptian friendship.
Underfoot: no concrete face, just a vast bank of rock and clay.
fun_fact: The first man asked to dam the Nile here, the scientist Ibn al-Haytham around 1011, decided it was impossible and pretended to be mad to escape the caliph's anger; under house arrest he wrote his famous Book of Optics.
narration:
You are standing on the Aswan High Dam. To the south is Lake Nasser, about 500 kilometres long, reaching into Sudan. To the north, the Nile runs on to the sea, and it will never flood again.

It is not a concrete wall. It is a mountain of rock and clay, nearly 4 kilometres long and 111 metres high.

The first dam here was British, finished in 1902, 7 kilometres downstream. The plan for this giant came from a Greek Egyptian engineer, Adrian Daninos. When America and Britain withdrew their offer of loans in 1956, Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal, and the Soviet Union stepped in with money and engineers. Construction ran from 1960 to 1970.

The results are mixed. No more famines from low floods, two harvests a year, and electricity from the turbines. But the fertile silt now settles at the bottom of the lake, farmers need fertiliser, the Delta coast is eroding, and about 100,000 Nubians lost their homes. At the west end, look for the tall lotus-shaped tower, the monument to Soviet Egyptian friendship.

period: Roman, Augustus, about 30 BC; Beit el-Wali, Ramesses II, 13th century BC
summary: Nubia's largest free-standing temple, moved in 13,000 blocks by West Germany, with a pig ban and a Christian king's boast in Greek.
look: On the rescue site of New Kalabsha beside the High Dam, usually reached by a short boat ride, stand three monuments: the big temple of Mandulis (Kalabsha), 76 metres long, with its pylon facing the water; the small rock-cut temple of Beit el-Wali behind it, built by Ramesses II, with brightly painted scenes; and the Kiosk of Qertassi with Hathor-headed columns.
story:
Mandulis was a Nubian sun god, and his temple was begun under Augustus around 30 BC over an older sanctuary of Amenhotep II, and never finished. It stood about 50 km south of Aswan. After UNESCO's appeal in 1960, West Germany chose to fund and run this rescue itself. The firm Hochtief started dismantling in 1961 from barges while the temple was still partly under water, numbering 13,000 blocks. It was rebuilt here in 1962-63. In thanks, Egypt gave Germany one of its gates, now in Berlin.

Look for two inscriptions: a decree of the Roman governor Aurelius Besarion of AD 250 banning pigs from the temple, and the victory text of Silko, a 5th-century Christian king of the Nobades, written in Greek, with an image of him on horseback in Roman dress.
details: In the temple: the Silko inscription with the king on horseback; ask the guard to show you.
Beit el-Wali: Ramesses II's Nubian campaign and tribute scenes, still brightly coloured.
The Kiosk of Qertassi: Hathor-headed columns at its entrance.
The view across the water to the High Dam.
fun_fact: Silko called himself, in Greek, 'kinglet of the Nobades and all the Ethiopians': a Nubian king boasting in the language of Homer.
narration:
This is New Kalabsha, a rescue site beside the High Dam. The big temple belongs to Mandulis, a Nubian sun god. It was begun under the emperor Augustus and never finished, and it once stood 50 kilometres south of here. In the early 1960s West Germany paid to save it. Engineers cut it into 13,000 numbered blocks, some lifted from barges while the temple was still under water, and rebuilt it here.

Inside, look for two odd inscriptions: a Roman governor's order of AD 250 banning pigs from the temple, and the boast of Silko, a Christian Nubian king, written in Greek. Then visit little Beit el Wali behind it, with Ramesses the Second's painted Nubian tribute.

summary: Thomas Cook's grand winter hotel, where Agatha Christie stayed and set part of Death on the Nile, with Aswan's most famous sunset terrace.
look: The historic terracotta-coloured palace wing stands on a granite outcrop at the southern end of the Corniche, facing Elephantine; a 1961 tower wing rises behind it. The terrace looks over the river and the boulders. Since May 2026 the hotel has been run by Mandarin Oriental, with the tower wing under renovation. Non-guests usually need a booking and a minimum spend for the terrace.
story:
Thomas Cook built the Cataract Hotel in 1899 for European winter travellers, and it opened on 8 January 1900 with 120 rooms. It did so well that a third storey and a dining room were added in 1902. The guest list reads like a history lesson: Tsar Nicholas II, Winston Churchill, Howard Carter, Margaret Thatcher, Jimmy Carter, Francois Mitterrand, Princess Diana and Agatha Christie, who set part of Death on the Nile here. The 1978 film was shot at the hotel.

It was closed for restoration from 2008 to 2011, and is due to be renamed Mandarin Oriental Old Cataract in 2027.
details: The terrace at sunset: Elephantine's boulders and the feluccas below.
The 1902 dining room with its high dome, if you are allowed a look.
From the river: the terracotta facade on its granite rock.
Look across to Elephantine's southern tip: the Nilometer and the Khnum temple.
fun_fact: In the novel, Poirot's steamer sails upriver from near Aswan to Wadi Halfa; that whole stretch of river now lies under Lake Nasser.
narration:
The grand terracotta building on the rocks is the Old Cataract Hotel. Thomas Cook built it for wealthy European winter visitors, and it opened in January 1900. It was such a success that two years later another storey was added.

Its guest book is a history lesson: Tsar Nicholas the Second, Winston Churchill, Howard Carter, Princess Diana, and Agatha Christie, who set part of Death on the Nile here. The 1978 film was shot here too.

The terrace is the place for sunset. Non-guests usually need a booking and a minimum spend, so ask at the gate. From the terrace, look straight down at the dark boulders of Elephantine: Poirot saw the same view.

summary: Spices, hibiscus and baskets in the souq, then painted Nubian houses, crocodiles and real hospitality across the river.
look: The souq street runs parallel to the Corniche, one block back from the river, southwards from near the railway station: stalls of spices, dried hibiscus, dates, baskets, scarves and galabiyas. Gharb Soheil is a Nubian village on the west bank upstream of the city, reached by boat; its lanes of painted houses climb from the landing towards the desert.
story:
Aswan's souq is gentler than Cairo's bazaars. Hibiscus is one of the region's signature crops: dried red flowers sold by weight and brewed as karkade, hot or iced. Look also for dom-palm fruit, henna, spices, Nubian baskets and colourful scarves. Bargaining is expected and friendly: smile, offer less, and be ready to walk on.

Gharb Soheil is one of the Nubian villages that still sits on the river. Houses are painted in blues, yellows and pinks, with patterns, birds and boats. A stuffed crocodile over a door is an old Nubian charm against evil, and many households keep live young crocodiles to show visitors. You can drink tea in a family guesthouse, get a henna design or ride a camel.

Parts of the visit are staged for tourists, but the hospitality is real. Nubians in Egypt live mostly around Aswan and in the villages near Kom Ombo where many were resettled in the 1960s. Sailing back at dusk is part of the pleasure.
details: In the souq: heaps of dried red hibiscus flowers; ask to taste the karkade before you buy.
Dom-palm fruit: hard, brown and faintly gingerbread-flavoured, a local snack.
In Gharb Soheil: look up for a stuffed crocodile over a doorway, a charm against evil.
Painted house walls: boats, birds and geometric bands in blue, yellow and white.
Ask before photographing people, especially women and children.
fun_fact: The dom palm is called the gingerbread tree in English; baskets of its fruit were among the food left in Tutankhamun's tomb.
narration:
Two faces of living Aswan: the souq in town, and a Nubian village across the river.

In the souq, look for heaps of dried red hibiscus flowers. Brewed, they make karkade, Aswan's ruby-red drink, served hot or ice cold. Next to them you will find hard brown dom palm fruit, which tastes faintly of gingerbread, as well as henna, spices, baskets and scarves. Bargaining is expected and friendly: smile, offer less, and be ready to walk on. It is far more relaxed than in Cairo.

Gharb Soheil, on the west bank, is a Nubian village with houses painted blue, yellow and pink, decorated with patterns, birds and boats. You may see a stuffed crocodile over a door, an old Nubian charm against evil, and some families keep live young crocodiles to show visitors. You can sit for tea, get a henna design, or ride a camel.

Yes, parts of it are staged for tourists. But the welcome is real. On the boat back at dusk, look at the west bank: the painted houses turn gold, then pink, then dark.
